introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics 3 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. For your guidance the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.
enonce_intro_markdown: A particle $P$ moves with constant angular velocity $\omega$ on the polar curve with equation $r = f(\theta)$. At time $t$, the transverse component of the acceleration of $P$ is $2a\omega^2\cos\theta$, where $a$ is a positive constant. Initially $P$ is at the point with polar coordinates $\left(a, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Show that the radial component of the velocity of $P$ is $a\omega\cos\theta$. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
In polar coordinates the velocity has radial component $\dot r$ and transverse component $r\dot\theta$, and the transverse component of the acceleration is

$$r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta.$$

The angular velocity is constant, $\dot\theta=\omega$, so $\ddot\theta=0$ and the transverse acceleration is $2\omega\dot r$. Equating with the given value:

$$2\omega\dot r = 2a\omega^2\cos\theta \;\Longrightarrow\; \dot r = a\omega\cos\theta.$$

So the radial component of the velocity is $\dot r = a\omega\cos\theta$.

By the chain rule, $\dot r = \dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta = \omega\,\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}$. Using part (i):

$$\omega\frac{dr}{d\theta} = a\omega\cos\theta \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{dr}{d\theta} = a\cos\theta \qquad(\omega\neq0).$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Find the polar equation of the path of $P$. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Integrate $\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}=a\cos\theta$:

$$r = a\sin\theta + C.$$

Initially $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$ and $r=a$, so $a = a\sin\dfrac\pi2 + C = a + C$, giving $C=0$. The polar equation of the path is

$$r = a\sin\theta,$$

a circle of diameter $a$ through the pole (Cartesian form $x^2+y^2=ay$).

questions.enonce_markdown: Find, in terms of $\theta$, $\omega$, the radial acceleration of $P$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The radial component of the acceleration is $\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2$. From part (i), $\dot r = a\omega\cos\theta$, so with $\dot\theta=\omega$:

$$\ddot r = \frac{d}{dt}\left(a\omega\cos\theta\right) = -a\omega\sin\theta\cdot\dot\theta = -a\omega^2\sin\theta.$$

Also $r\dot\theta^2 = a\sin\theta\cdot\omega^2$. Therefore

$$\text{radial acceleration} = \ddot r - r\dot\theta^2 = -a\omega^2\sin\theta - a\omega^2\sin\theta = -2a\omega^2\sin\theta,$$

of magnitude $2a\omega^2\sin\theta$ directed towards the pole.
